canonical_statement: The review aimed to quantify associations between CCL5 levels and unfavorable disease progression and mortality in patients with respiratory viral infections.
The systematic review and meta-analysis followed PRISMA guidance and was registered in PROSPERO as CRD420251109172.

The authors searched Medline/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, CABI Digital Library, and Global Health (Ovid) through October 1, 2025, with no language or geographic restrictions and manual reference-list screening.

Eligible studies were observational cohort or case-control studies of patients with confirmed respiratory viral infection that measured CCL5 in biological samples and reported severity or mortality data sufficient to calculate an effect size.

population.label: Patients with confirmed respiratory viral infection
inclusion_criteria: CCL5 measured in a biological sample
Clinical severity or mortality outcome with effect-size data

canonical_statement: Reviews, nonhuman studies, studies without a relevant comparison group, and reports without extractable outcome data were excluded.

population.label: Candidate reports screened for the review

canonical_statement: Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data; disagreements were resolved by consensus or a third reviewer, and authors were contacted up to three times when essential data were missing.
Risk of bias was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, study quality was categorized as high (≥7 stars), moderate (5-6), or low (≤4), and certainty of evidence was evaluated with GRADE.

Unfavorable disease progression was defined as a composite of moderate and severe clinical progression, with severe events including ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, ARDS, or study-defined severe/critical illness.

outcome.definition: Composite endpoint: severe progression included ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, ARDS, or study-defined severe/critical illness; moderate progression primarily included hospital admission or study-defined moderate illness.

canonical_statement: Mortality encompassed all-cause death, including in-hospital, 28-day, or 30-day mortality.

The primary pooled effect measure was the odds ratio; reported hazard ratios and relative risks for rare outcomes were treated as approximations of odds ratios, and pooled estimates used a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model.

Heterogeneity was assessed with Cochran Q and I²; subgroup interaction tests, univariable REML meta-regression with Knapp-Hartung adjustment, funnel plots, Begg and Egger tests, trim-and-fill, and leave-one-out analyses were used for heterogeneity, publication-bias, and robustness assessments.
The search identified 2787 records and ultimately included 18 studies in the quantitative synthesis; screening agreement was κ=0.77 and full-text agreement was κ=0.92.
The 18 included studies comprised 2376 patients; median study age was 58.2 years (range, 0.08-65.0), and 1278 of 2126 patients with sex data (60.1%) were male.

canonical_statement: Virus type did not significantly modify the unfavorable-progression association (P=.47 for interaction), and age group did not significantly modify it (P=.66 for interaction).
For unfavorable disease progression, meta-regression found no significant modification by publication year (coefficient −0.015; 95% CI −0.049 to 0.019; P=.35).
For unfavorable disease progression, meta-regression found no significant modification by country income status (coefficient 0.011; 95% CI −0.403 to 0.425; P=.95).
For unfavorable disease progression, meta-regression found no significant modification by study sample size (coefficient −0.0006; 95% CI −0.0028 to 0.0016; P=.57).
For mortality, meta-regression found no significant modification by publication year (coefficient −0.102; 95% CI −0.240 to 0.037; P=.12).
For mortality, meta-regression found no significant modification by study sample size (coefficient −0.0006; 95% CI −0.0018 to 0.0007; P=.30).
Restricting the disease-progression analysis to studies reporting odds ratios did not materially alter the association (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.72-0.86).

canonical_statement: For unfavorable disease progression, Begg (z=−1.56; P=.16) and Egger (z=−1.53; P=.13) tests did not indicate funnel-plot asymmetry, and trim-and-fill imputed zero missing studies.
For mortality, Begg and Egger tests each yielded z=0.30 and P=.76, and trim-and-fill imputed zero missing studies.
Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses indicated that no single study drove the pooled unfavorable-progression or mortality estimates.
Twelve of 18 included studies (67%) were rated high quality by the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, 6 (33%) were rated moderate quality, and none were rated low quality.
The 6 moderate-quality studies lacked statistical adjustment for confounders, whereas all 12 high-quality studies performed multivariable adjustment.
Nine of 18 studies did not report consecutive recruitment, which the authors identified as a potential source of selection bias.
The authors rated certainty of evidence as moderate for both unfavorable disease progression and mortality after upgrading from low on the basis of effect magnitude and low heterogeneity.

The authors concluded that elevated CCL5 levels were consistently associated with favorable clinical outcomes and survival in respiratory viral infections and may reflect a proficient antiviral immune response rather than pathogenic hyperinflammation.
The authors proposed CCL5 as a potential prognostic biomarker for patient risk stratification but called for prospective multicenter validation with standardized assays and clinical cutoffs.

The authors proposed investigating therapeutic strategies to augment CCL5 responses in patients with demonstrated deficiencies, while discussing context-dependent CCR5 blockade as a separate hypothesis for established ARDS.
The number of studies was small for some subgroups, especially mortality, limiting detailed stratified analyses.

CCL5 assay techniques and disease-severity definitions varied, and the composite progression endpoint combined ICU admission, mechanical ventilation, ARDS, hospitalization, and study-defined severity; the authors noted that low statistical heterogeneity could therefore reflect overaggregation rather than clinical homogeneity.

Pooling odds ratios, hazard ratios, and relative risks from different regression models and combining studies with different covariate-adjustment structures limited interpretability; the authors advised treating the pooled estimate as a broad association rather than a precise unified target metric.
Publication bias could not be excluded despite negative formal asymmetry tests.
Because the evidence base was observational, residual confounding remained possible and causality could not be established.

The companion eTable reports 11 studies (n=1241) for unfavorable disease progression, whereas the main article reports 11 studies (n=1214) for the same pooled analysis.
